objectives: Reach a negotiated settlement with the UK that allows the EU to proceed with a materially unchanged core measure (50% out-of-quota bound rate preserved; overall TRQ volume close to 400,000t globally) while avoiding UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions.

Prevent the UK from joining a joint FTA/retaliation front with Japan and Korea over the FTA-disapplication text; if possible, resolve or soften that specific element bilaterally with the UK so it has no reason to align with them.

Keep any UK-specific concession narrow and technically justifiable (e.g. tied to product-line concentration or a country-specific sub-quota) rather than a broad political carve-out, so Turkey and Korea cannot credibly claim parity in their separate processes.

Explore linking this negotiation to the UK's own parallel steel safeguard, securing at least a soft understanding on EU exporters' existing country allocations there, without letting the talks become hostage to that separate file.
Protect the Commission's negotiating credibility and the June Council timetable — arrive at either a clean deal or a clearly-documented impasse that Council can act on without member-state revolt.
Preserve the working relationship with my UK counterpart for the ongoing goods agenda beyond this file.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement (or a managed non-settlement) that lets the EU implement its steel measure on the schedule needed for Council sign-off in June, with the UK not withdrawing concessions and not joining a Japan/Korea joint action against the FTA-disapplication provisions; ideally achieved through a bounded, technical concession (product carve-out, UK sub-quota, review clause) rather than broad compensation elsewhere in the schedule. Failure: no deal and the UK retaliates and/or joins a Japan-Korea coalition to contest the FTA disapplication; or a deal is reached that is generous enough to invite Turkey/Korea to demand equivalent treatment, or that Brussels' member states (producers) reject at Council.
declaration.approach: Open by firmly grounding the measure in trade-defence logic (overcapacity, non-market-economy sourcing) to signal the out-of-quota rate and overall architecture are not up for renegotiation. Offer flexibility early on the items cheapest to the EU but valuable to the UK: duration/review clause, product-line carve-outs where UK exports are concentrated, and a UK-specific share or sub-quota within the global TRQ (cheaper than cross-schedule compensation and less likely to be replicable by Turkey/Korea, since it can be framed as reflecting UK's narrow product concentration rather than a general precedent). Treat the FTA-disapplication clause as the most politically sensitive item for the UK and look for a bespoke solution there (e.g. phased application, TCA-specific carve-out, or linkage to reciprocal treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard) specifically to remove the UK's incentive to combine with Japan and Korea. Avoid setting explicit numeric offers before hearing the UK's opening position and capital's steer; use Phase 2 consultations to test Brussels' real room for manoeuvre on volume vs. carve-outs vs. review clauses. Keep language on the record cautious and technical, since Turkey, Korea, India and Japan are watching this process even though handled separately.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A meaningful, defensible increase in tariff-free access — via a UK-specific quota share, product carve-outs in lines of concentrated UK production, a review clause, and preferably removal or softening of the FTA-disapplication provision to preserve TCA-based access. Also wants assurance on reciprocal treatment for EU exporters under its own steel safeguard, and is under domestic pressure given employment concentration at a small number of sites.

parties.who: Japan and Korea (not at the table, but influencing UK)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To draw the UK into a joint challenge against the EU's FTA-disapplication text, using collective pressure to protect their own FTA-based access and set a precedent against the EU using Article XXVIII to strip third-country preferences.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (separate Article XXVIII claims)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger absolute volume protection given their bigger shipment volumes to the EU; will watch the UK settlement closely and seek at least equivalent treatment if the UK secures a generous country-specific allocation or carve-out.

A durable, WTO-defensible measure that protects EU steel producers from non-market-economy overcapacity, delivered on the June timetable, without triggering costly retaliation or destabilising the broader EU-UK relationship; steel-producing member states will resist generous carve-outs, steel-consuming member states will want more access preserved.

parties.who: EU domestic constituencies (steel producers vs. consuming manufacturers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want the highest possible out-of-quota rate and lowest TRQ; downstream manufacturers want broader access preserved, including via the UK, to avoid input cost increases.

objectives: Secure UK agreement to the Article XXVIII modification within the four-round window so the Council can vote in June.

Preserve the structural integrity of the new import regime: a meaningful out-of-quota rate, a workable TRQ volume, and an allocation method that does not undermine the regime's ability to constrain non-market-economy overcapacity.

Give the UK a country-specific or effectively ring-fenced share of the TRQ (rather than pure global first-come-first-served) as the core compensation, sized to reflect its principal supplying interest, without setting a precedent that other claimants (Turkey, Korea) can leverage into equal or larger asks.
Retain flexibility on the FTA-disapplication provision — willing to soften or delay its application to the UK specifically, using this as a negotiating lever rather than a fixed demand.

Avoid opening compensation on unrelated tariff lines if possible; prefer to settle via TRQ design (volume, country share, administration, review clause) rather than concessions elsewhere in the schedule.

Manage linkage to the UK's own steel safeguard and TCA treatment of EU exporters carefully — resist letting the UK use its reciprocal measure as leverage to extract more than the trade volumes justify.
Keep member states (producers and downstream users) and the Trade Policy Committee comfortable with the final terms so Council approval is not put at risk.
Avoid triggering a UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, which would create a second front while the EU is already exposed to US retaliation threats.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a signed settlement within four rounds giving the UK a defined, bankable share of the TRQ (or equivalent guaranteed access) that is clearly less than its historic 2.4mt but enough to be presented domestically as protecting the core of UK-EU steel trade, with the out-of-quota rate and global quota structure otherwise intact, no broad reopening of unrelated schedule concessions, and no UK retaliation. Failure: no deal, forcing the Council vote on the harsher first-notified terms (400kt global FCFS, 50% out-of-quota, no carve-outs), followed by UK withdrawal of concessions against EU exporters, escalating a second trade dispute alongside US pressure, and drawing criticism from the Trade Policy Committee for mismanaging a foreseeable negotiation. Partial failure: a deal that is agreed but is seen internally as too generous to the UK, undermining the regime's stated purpose of curbing overcapacity and inviting similar asks from Turkey/Korea/Japan/India.
declaration.approach: Start firm on the core architecture (50% out-of-quota rate, global TRQ ceiling near 400,000t as the anchor) to protect Council mandate credibility, but signal early that country-specific allocation for the UK, administration method, review clauses, and FTA treatment are genuinely negotiable — these are cheaper concessions for the EU than raising the overall volume or lowering the out-of-quota rate. Use the FTA-disapplication clause as a bargaining chip: offer to exempt or phase it for the UK in exchange for UK acceptance of the volume and rate. Try to keep any volume increase targeted and framed as a UK-specific carve-out within the existing 400,000t envelope (or a modest increase justified by UK's concentrated product mix) rather than a general loosening that Turkey/Korea could cite. Avoid discussing compensation on unrelated tariff lines unless TRQ-design concessions prove insufficient. Watch for signals in Phase 2/3 about UK's true walk-away threshold — the analysis suggests no-deal hurts the UK more, so I can afford to hold firm through at least two rounds before offering my real reservation position, saving room to move only enough to close by round four. Coordinate implicitly with likely Council concerns by not conceding anything that member state producers would see as gutting the regime's purpose.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A UK-specific quota share close to historical trade volumes (2.4mt), a low or zero out-of-quota rate within that share, exemption from the FTA-disapplication clause, a review/sunset clause, and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard. They face real pressure since no-deal damages UK steel more than EU, but they will not want to be seen capitulating either, and will likely link EU treatment to how the UK treats EU steel under its own measure and TCA.

Watching this negotiation closely as a precedent; will want any UK country-specific allocation to not disadvantage their own larger volumes, and may push for proportionate or larger shares in their separate tracks. I should avoid setting terms that are trivially copied by them at greater cost to the EU.

parties.who: EU member states / Trade Policy Committee (steel producers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum protection — high out-of-quota rate, tight global volume, minimal carve-outs, strict rules of origin/circumvention provisions, and disapplication of FTA benefits to prevent transshipment. They will resist any deal seen as reopening the door to significant tariff-free UK volumes.

parties.who: EU member states / downstream manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to affordable steel inputs, so they will favour a larger TRQ, lower out-of-quota rate, and preservation of UK supply given integrated supply chains, creating internal EU tension I must manage when finalising terms.

A concluded deal by June that can be defended as both protecting EU industry from overcapacity and demonstrating orderly, rules-based trade diplomacy — avoiding a high-profile no-deal outcome, especially while US retaliation is already a live threat.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) large enough to preserve current or near-current tariff-free volumes for UK exporters, with reference to the 2.4mt historical trade flow rather than a share of the reduced 400,000t pool

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel, arguing the UK should be treated as at least equivalent to EEA given the depth of the TCA and the UK's own parallel safeguard action against the same overcapacity problem

Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure isn't a permanent ratchet, plus carve-outs or protected sub-quotas for product lines where UK exports are concentrated (since UK volumes are narrower/deeper than Turkey/Korea)
Extract meaningful compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if volume/allocation asks cannot be fully met, to offset value lost to UK industry
Preserve UK optionality on its own steel safeguard vis-à-vis EU exporters as a bargaining chip, without triggering an unnecessary two-front dispute
Avoid a no-deal outcome that forces the UK into retaliatory withdrawal of concessions, which hits UK downstream/consuming industries and escalates with the EU on multiple files
Keep Geneva working relationship with EU counterpart intact for other goods-file business regardless of outcome

Manage Japan/Korea/Turkey relationship carefully: avoid formal coordination that could slow or complicate the UK-EU bilateral track before June, but do not alienate them either, since UK may want their support later or need to avoid being isolated if no deal is reached
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement before or by Round 4 that gives the UK either a country-specific quota share materially above a pro-rata population/trade-based split of 400,000t (ideally closer to historical UK volumes or a credibly growing baseline), preserves TCA-equivalent tariff treatment for UK steel (or secures a carve-out/phase-in), includes a review clause and reasonable duration, and/or is paired with real compensation - all landing before London concludes it must retaliate. Failure: no deal, forcing the EU's 400,000t global FCFS/50% regime into force, UK forced into a slow, costly, six-month-delayed retaliation that damages UK-EU relations across multiple files and doesn't actually restore lost market access, while UK steel industry suffers real damage in the interim from lost EU access. Partial success: a deal that stops the worst (FTA disapplication, zero country share) even if volumes remain below status quo.
declaration.approach: Open by testing EU flexibility without revealing UK's true floor - use Phase 1 to press on the weakest points of the EU's opening offer (FCFS allocation disadvantages a lower-volume, concentrated exporter like the UK relative to Turkey/Korea; disapplying TCA is legally and politically provocative given the depth of UK-EU integration and the UK's own parallel measure targeting the same non-market-economy overcapacity, meaning the EU and UK are natural allies against the real target, not each other). Use consultation phases to relay EU's actual room for movement to London honestly, and to seek a settlement figure/mandate from London since none has been given yet - flag the retaliation risk and the Japan/Korea pressure without committing to joint action. Sequence asks: country-specific share first (concrete, quantifiable), then FTA/TCA treatment (principled, high salience), then review clause and duration (lower cost for EU to concede, useful as a face-saving addition), holding compensation and safeguard-linkage as trade space for a late round. Avoid early threats I can't back without capital authority; keep the Japan/Korea joint-dispute option in reserve as leverage to mention only if talks stall, since triggering it risks losing control of the process and merging UK's narrower, deeper interest into a larger, harder-to-manage multilateral fight.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude a defensible package by June that Council/member states will approve, likely wants to hold the line on the 50% rate and global FCFS quota as leverage but has room to trade allocation method, some country share, review clause, or minor compensation; under real time pressure which UK can use

Balance steel-producing member states (want maximum protection, minimal concessions) against steel-consuming member states (want cheaper input access, more quota); want the file closed on schedule without opening new internal fights

Protect UK steel jobs and production sites concentrated in specific locations; will want tangible volume/value guarantees, likely reluctant to authorise retaliation given knock-on costs to UK consuming industries and TCA relationship, but under domestic political pressure to be seen defending steel
Wants UK to join a joint FTA-disapplication retaliation/dispute to pressure the EU; primarily serving its own principal-supplier interest, sees UK as useful ally to add weight
Similar to Japan - larger volume exporter than UK, wants coordinated pressure on the EU, has more leverage alone than the UK does and may push hardest for joint action
Largest affected volume alongside Korea, likely pursuing its own bilateral track with the EU but with shared interest in undermining the global FCFS/FTA-disapplication approach
Smaller/separate interest, likely watching precedent set by UK/Turkey/Korea outcomes for its own claim

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK quota share within the EU TRQ (not global FCFS), sized to protect the bulk of current UK export volumes (target 2.4m tonnes or as close as achievable), rather than accepting UK exporters competing globally against Turkey/Korea/India/Japan/China-linked volumes
Preserve UK access at zero or low duty within quota, and push for a lower/staged out-of-quota rate rather than 50%

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA preferential treatment for UK-origin steel specifically - argue UK should not be treated as a third-country FTA partner given the parallel bilateral dynamic and TCA relationship
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration (not indefinite) so the regime can be revisited as market conditions change
Get carve-outs or enhanced allocation for product lines most critical to at-risk UK plants
Extract compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if quota/allocation terms cannot be improved sufficiently

Use UK's own safeguard country-specific quota for EU exporters as a bargaining chip - only concede improved EU access in our safeguard in exchange for real, substantial EU concessions on the TRQ terms
Avoid a scenario where both the EU measure lands badly on UK industry AND we fail to secure reciprocal protection in our own safeguard
Keep optionality on withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions as leverage/backstop if no deal
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share materially above what pure global FCFS competition would deliver, preserved TCA/FTA-equivalent treatment (or a clearly better carve-out than other third countries), a bounded duration with review clause, and if volume/rate terms are still worse than status quo, compensation or safeguard reciprocity that gives ministers a credible story that the deal supports the two at-risk plants' investment case. Failure: UK steel treated identically to global first-come-first-served competitors, FTA disapplication proceeds against the UK specifically, no review clause, no compensation, and industry concludes the deal does not change the investment calculus - leaving ministers to face plant closures with no multilateral offset and having potentially given away safeguard concessions for nothing.
declaration.approach: Lead with the UK's principal supplying interest status and the asymmetric harm point (75% of UK exports by value at stake), and frame the ask as proportionate compensation for substantially impairing an existing concession rather than a favour. Prioritise the country-specific quota share as the primary ask since it is the single lever most likely to preserve actual export volume, and treat the out-of-quota rate and duration/review clause as secondary but still valuable asks. Hold the safeguard reciprocity offer in reserve - do not table it early, only deploy it in later rounds if the EU shows movement on quota share/FTA treatment, to avoid conceding UK leverage cheaply. Use the parallel UK Article XXVIII/safeguard process as leverage: signal (without over-committing) that UK measures affecting EU exporters are also live and could be adjusted either favourably or unfavourably depending on how this negotiation goes. Avoid revealing the subsidy backstop or the plant closure specifics to the EU side - keep that as an internal ministerial contingency, not a negotiating card, since disclosing weakness could reduce urgency for the EU to concede. Escalate gradually across the four rounds: probe in round 1, test EU flexibility on quota structure and FTA disapplication in round 2, make the safeguard-reciprocity offer conditional in round 3 if warranted, and only accept in round 4 if the package is defensible to ministers and industry.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To finalise a legally durable TRQ regime by June in time for Council vote, minimise compensation payouts across all claimants (UK, Turkey, Korea, India, Japan), maintain a defensible 'non-market economy overcapacity' justification, keep the regime as close to their original 50%/400kt global FCFS proposal as possible, and avoid setting a precedent of generous country-specific carve-outs that other claimants (especially Turkey and Korea, who ship more volume) will then demand too.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council/mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Strong protection against import surges, high out-of-quota rates, tight global quota volumes - pushing the Commission toward a tougher line and less generous UK carve-out.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: More generous quota volumes and continued affordable input access, potentially sympathetic to preserving UK supply given integrated supply chains - possible internal EU tension we can exploit rhetorically.

Maximum preserved tariff-free access to the EU market, certainty/duration to justify investment, and will judge government success by whether the deal changes the closure calculus - not by process quality.

parties.who: UK downstream steel-consuming/manufacturing sectors and DBT colleagues handling the UK's own safeguard
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to competitively priced EU steel imports under the UK's own safeguard measure; will resist us giving away too much EU quota share domestically without commensurate EU concessions.

Their own country-specific shares or compensation; Turkey and Korea's larger volumes give them more leverage and their outcomes may set comparators/precedents that affect what the EU is willing to offer the UK.

public_message: The EU recognises the UK's principal supplying interest in these tariff lines and comes to this negotiation in good faith, seeking a settlement that provides substantially equivalent compensation rather than proceeding unilaterally. As an opening position: we propose increasing the overall TRQ pool from 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes, moving from global first-come-first-served allocation to a country-specific allocation, with a dedicated UK tranche of 300,000 tonnes reflecting recent trade shares. We propose retaining the 50% out-of-quota rate at this stage, but with a review clause after three years. On the FTA disapplication point, we are prepared to discuss carving the UK out of that provision, conditional on reciprocal treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard quota allocations. We see this as a starting point for discussion, not a final offer, and want to work through allocation method, duration and enforcement provisions with you over the coming rounds.

other_terms: UK-origin steel exempted from FTA disapplication clause, conditional on reciprocal EU treatment under the UK's own safeguard measure
Willingness to discuss product-line carve-outs reflecting the UK's narrower product concentration
Joint work on anti-circumvention/origin verification provisions

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter-proposal pressing for a larger UK tranche, a lower or phased out-of-quota rate, and unconditional removal of the FTA disapplication as it applies to the UK
expectations.why: The UK's domestic political pressure is concentrated on a small number of production sites and on TCA preference erosion; they will want visible wins on tranche size and FTA treatment before conceding on rate or duration

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that a country-specific allocation and conditional FTA carve-out are within mandate
expectations.why: Moving off global FCFS and touching the FTA disapplication text goes beyond the bare notified measure, so capital sign-off is needed before further concessions in later rounds

private_rationale: Opening above the fallback (400k/global/50%/no review) signals genuine willingness to negotiate, which is necessary to keep the UK from joining a Japan/Korea coalition against the FTA disapplication clause. Offering conditional UK exemption from that clause specifically targets the retaliation risk we most want to avoid, while tying it to reciprocity on the UK's own safeguard gives us leverage on their parallel Article XXVIII process. Keeping the out-of-quota rate at 50% and duration at 3 years for now preserves room to make concessions in later rounds rather than conceding too much in round 1.

public_message: We welcome the EU's acknowledgement of the UK's principal supplying interest, but the opening offer does not come close to substantially equivalent compensation. The UK exported 2.4 million tonnes to the EU annually over the last three years at zero duty. A 300,000 tonne country-specific tranche represents an 87% cut to that access, dressed up as an increase to the overall pool. That is not compensation, it is a fraction of the loss. Our opening position: a UK-specific tranche of at least 2.0 million tonnes within an expanded global pool, reflecting our recent trade share, not a token allocation. On the out-of-quota rate, 50% is prohibitive and effectively closes the market above the quota - we need a materially lower rate, and would want to discuss a rate closer to 15-20% for volumes above the UK tranche as part of any landing zone. We do not accept a three-year gap before review; if this regime is to be workable we need a review after twelve months with an automatic mechanism to adjust the UK tranche in line with actual trade flows, not a discretionary re-opening. On FTA disapplication: the UK should be excluded from that provision outright, as a matter of the TCA relationship, not as something conditional on unrelated concessions in our own safeguard. We are willing to discuss the treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure, but as a separate strand on its own merits, not as a precondition for basic fairness here. We want to move quickly given the timeline you're working to, but the current numbers would do serious damage to our industry and we need to see the EU move substantially before we can bring this back to capitals as a credible basis.

other_terms: Review after 12 months with automatic adjustment mechanism tied to trailing trade volumes, not purely discretionary renegotiation
UK fully carved out of FTA disapplication provision, unconditional on other issues
Treatment of EU exporters under UK safeguard quota to be discussed as a separate, parallel strand
Enforcement/circumvention provisions to be based on objective origin verification, not discretionary suspension of quota access

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that moves the UK tranche up materially from 300,000 tonnes and softens on the out-of-quota rate, while likely holding firm on FTA disapplication linkage
expectations.why: The EU needs a deal by June for the Council vote and has signalled this is an opening position, so they have room to move, but will want to protect the FTA linkage as leverage on their own steel safeguard interests

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation of a walk-away threshold on tranche size and out-of-quota rate, and guidance on how far to concede on the safeguard reciprocity linkage
expectations.why: I have not been given a settlement figure and need capital to set the floor before I can meaningfully trade off tranche size against rate and duration in later rounds

private_rationale: Anchoring high is necessary given the EU's opening bid is far below any credible measure of substantial equivalence - 300,000 tonnes against a 2.4 million tonne trade flow is a starting point designed to be negotiated up, so matching with a low counter would concede too much ground too early. I've avoided giving away the safeguard reciprocity point for free, since London hasn't authorised trading UK safeguard treatment of EU exporters against this file, and conflating the two plays into the EU's hands. I've also flagged the Japan/Korea joint dispute angle only implicitly by taking a hard line on FTA disapplication, without committing to coordinate with them until I have capital's steer - that's a separate lever I don't want to burn early or let capital feel boxed into by Geneva-level signalling.

report: Opening exchange completed. We tabled 500k tonne global pool, country-specific allocation with a 300k tonne UK tranche, 50% out-of-quota rate retained, three-year review clause, and a conditional FTA carve-out linked to reciprocal treatment under the UK's own safeguard quotas. UK rejected this as far short of substantially equivalent compensation, noting their historical trade of 2.4mt/year. Their opening counter: UK-specific tranche of at least 2.0mt within an expanded global pool, out-of-quota rate of 15-20% for above-tranche volumes, a 12-month review with an automatic (non-discretionary) volume-adjustment mechanism, and an unconditional FTA carve-out delinked from the UK safeguard treatment of EU exporters. They did agree to discuss EU treatment under their own safeguard as a separate strand, which is useful — it suggests they don't want that issue to become a blocker, and reduces (for now) the risk of it being bundled into a joint action with Japan/Korea. No numbers were agreed; both sides marked this as opening positions only. UK signalled willingness to move quickly given our timeline, which is useful leverage but also means they expect us to move first and substantially.

recommendation.reasoning: The gap between opening positions (300k vs 2.0m tranche; 50% vs 15-20% out-of-quota; 3-year vs 12-month review) is wide but this is a first round and both sides marked their positions as opening only. There is no basis yet to accept or walk away. We should use round 2 to test how much movement is real versus rhetorical, and to start decoupling the FTA carve-out from the UK safeguard linkage, since the UK's willingness to treat that as a separate strand reduces the risk of a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA retaliation, which is a strategic priority for us independent of the tonnage numbers.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to move the UK tranche upward materially (indicative range 500k-700k) in round 2, without yet approaching UK's 2.0m ask, to test whether their number is a genuine floor or an opening gambit.
requests.why: We need room to demonstrate good faith and momentum given the June Council deadline, but should not concede too much too early — steel-producing member states (and the Commission's own overcapacity rationale) will resist a large tranche that undermines the TRQ's protective purpose.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on whether we can offer an unconditional FTA carve-out for the UK now, delinked from the UK safeguard question, in exchange for locking in the UK on tranche/rate numbers.
requests.why: The UK clearly wants this delinked and treating it as a standalone concession may be low-cost for us (UK is not an FTA overcapacity risk) while buying significant goodwill and reducing the risk of a joint EU-directed FTA dispute with Japan and Korea, which is a bigger strategic threat than the tonnage gap itself.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A steer on the out-of-quota rate floor Brussels can tolerate (is 30-35% conceivable as a landing zone, or must we hold at 50%?).
requests.why: The UK's 15-20% ask is far from our 50%; before round 2 I need to know the real limit so I don't have to walk back an offer that has already been tabled.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation on review clause design — can we accept a shorter review period (e.g., 18-24 months) with a data-triggered (not fully automatic) adjustment mechanism?
requests.why: A fully automatic mechanism removes Commission/Council discretion over future allocation, which member states are likely to resist; a data-triggered review with a presumption of adjustment may bridge the gap while preserving EU control.

private_rationale: The UK's numbers are an opening bid, but the tranche gap (300k vs 2.0m) is enormous and out-of-quota rate gap (50% vs 15-20%) is also large — settlement will likely land well below UK's ask but well above our opening offer, probably in the 700k-1.1m tonnage range with a rate in the 30-40% band and a review at 18-24 months, if political appetite exists. My real priority is preventing the UK from joining a Japan/Korea FTA retaliation coalition — the fact that UK treated the safeguard reciprocity issue as separable is a good early signal and I should reinforce that by offering to delink the FTA carve-out unconditionally if it helps lock other terms. I should not signal to the UK team how much I want that decoupling, since it's leverage for us. I'll manage the pace so we're seen moving in round 2 without giving away the landing zone yet — want Brussels to commit to real numbers before I make a bigger move at the table.

instruction: Good round. Move to a country-specific allocation with a UK tranche of 550,000 tonnes within a total pool of 650,000 tonnes (leaving headroom for Turkey/Korea/India/Japan allocations to be settled separately). Present this as a substantial, good-faith move from our opening 300k, but frame it as close to our practical ceiling rather than a first step in a long ladder — we want to compress the negotiation, not create a slow bidding war. Hold the allocation method as country-specific, not global-with-guaranteed-minimum: we need certainty on exposure, and a global pool with a UK floor effectively re-creates the FCFS risk we're trying to close off. On the out-of-quota rate, move from 50% to 35% as our next offer, framed as contingent on the UK accepting the tranche figure and a longer review period — do not go below 35% without further instruction. report: First round tabled. They explicitly framed this as an opening position, not final, and signalled willingness to move on allocation method, duration and enforcement. EU seemed to expect pushback and did not react defensively - they know their number is an opener. Timeline pressure is on their side more than ours; I have not signalled any UK deadline sensitivity.

recommendation.reasoning: EU's opening is far below any credible compensation figure - a 300,000t tranche against a 2.4mt baseline is not substantially equivalent by any reasonable reading of Article XXVIII. There is room to move in later rounds, but conceding early risks anchoring the EU's expectations too low given their tight June timeline works in our favour. Recommend continuing to press rather than accepting or walking away at this stage - we have not yet tested how far the EU will move, and they've signalled explicit flexibility on allocation, duration and FTA carve-out.

public_message: The EU has listened carefully to the UK's opening position and is prepared to move substantially. We now propose a total pool of 650,000 tonnes, with a dedicated UK country-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes - reflecting a serious, good-faith recalibration from our opening offer and, we would note, well above what a simple pro-rata read of global trade shares would suggest. On review, we propose an 18-month first review, built on a defined trade-share/utilisation formula, with a presumption of adjustment if UK utilisation exceeds the agreed threshold - this is a substantial improvement on our opening three-year proposal, though final trigger decisions remain with the Commission and Council, consistent with how EU tariff administration works. On the FTA disapplication point, we are now prepared to offer the UK an unconditional carve-out from that provision, delinked entirely from the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard measure. We would still hope to see that reciprocal treatment resolved favourably in parallel, as a matter of the overall relationship, but we are not making it a precondition here - we think this removes a significant source of friction and we hope it is recognised as such. We are not in a position to move to a global allocation with a floor; certainty on exposure is essential to us, and this is what allows us to move as far as we have on the tranche number. This offer holds together as a package - tranche and rate move together. We would ask the UK to engage substantively on both, rather than banking the tranche movement while continuing to hold at 15-20% on the rate.

public_message: We recognise that this is a substantial move from your opening position, and we say that genuinely - the shift on the out-of-quota rate and the unconditional FTA carve-out in particular are steps in the right direction, and we welcome both. But we need to be precise about where this leaves us. We'd like to understand that calculation in detail: what period, what product mix, and what weighting you've applied to arrive at 550,000, because our own figures based on the last three years' actual trade don't obviously support a number that low. On the out-of-quota rate, 35% is still prohibitive for most of the product lines in question - it doesn't function as a genuine safety valve above the tranche, it functions as a wall. On review, an 18 month first look with a defined formula is a better structure than a discretionary three-year gap, but a mechanism where the Commission and Council retain final say over triggering adjustment isn't materially different in practice from discretionary review - we'd want to understand exactly how the utilisation threshold and adjustment presumption would work, and whether there's any binding element at all, or whether it is Commission discretion by another name. We're not going to bank the movement on tranche and rate as separate wins - we understand this is a package, and we're prepared to move on the rate if we see the tranche move further toward reflecting actual trade, and if the review mechanism has real teeth. We're not in a position to move off our figures yet, but we want to flag that a package built around a higher tranche, a rate materially below 35%, and a genuinely binding 12-month review would be one we could credibly take back to capital. On the FTA carve-out, thank you for delinking it - we'll engage on the safeguard treatment of EU exporters separately and in good faith, on its own merits.

They reiterated 35% is 'a wall, not a safety valve' and want the rate materially lower. On review, they pushed back specifically on Commission/Council retaining final trigger discretion, calling it 'discretionary review by another name,' and want a genuinely binding mechanism with a 12-month first look. Importantly, they explicitly declined to 'bank' the tranche and rate moves separately, confirming they see this as a single package, and signalled that a package of (a) a higher tranche closer to actual trade, (b) a rate materially below 35%, and (c) a binding 12-month review would be capital-credible. They also confirmed good-faith engagement on EU treatment under the UK safeguard as a separate strand, which continues to reduce the risk of the UK aligning with Japan/Korea on a joint FTA-related retaliation — this is the second round in which they've kept that issue firmly decoupled, which I read as a genuine signal rather than tactical.

There is real engagement, not stonewalling, and both sides are treating this as a package rather than negotiating line by line, which is useful discipline. We should make one more substantial move in round 3 — combining a further tranche increase, a further rate cut, and a genuinely stronger review mechanism (short of full automaticity) — to test whether this produces UK movement off 2.0mt/15-20%, or whether we are approaching a real impasse. report: Second round saw significant EU movement from their opening position. New EU offer: total pool 650,000t, UK-specific tranche 550,000t (up from 300,000t), out-of-quota rate reduced to 35% (from 50%), an 18-month first review built on a trade-share/utilisation formula with a 'presumption of adjustment' if UK utilisation exceeds a threshold - though final trigger decisions remain with Commission/Council discretion. They have also now offered an unconditional UK carve-out from the FTA disapplication provision, delinked from reciprocal treatment of EU exporters under our safeguard - though they still 'hope' we resolve that favourably in parallel. They explicitly framed tranche and rate as a linked package and pushed us to move on rate if we want more tranche. They continue to resist global allocation with a floor, citing need for exposure certainty. I welcomed the FTA delinkage and the direction of travel on rate and review structure, but held our figures. I pushed hard on the calculation methodology behind 550,000t (period, product mix, weighting), noting our own trade-share reading doesn't support that number. I flagged that 35% still functions as a prohibitive wall rather than a safety valve, and that the 18-month review's 'presumption of adjustment' with Commission/Council final say may be discretionary review by another name - asked for detail on whether there's any binding element. I signalled we could bring back a credible package if tranche moves higher, rate moves materially below 35%, and the review has genuine binding teeth at 12 months - but did not concede on our own numbers or trade rate for volume explicitly. No agreement, as expected. This is now a real negotiation with a package on the table, not just an opening anchor - the EU has moved meaningfully but is still well short of our floor, particularly on tranche size and the bindingness of review provisions.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU has moved substantially from its opening position but the tranche (550,000t) still represents roughly a 77% cut from our actual 2.4mt baseline, and the 35% out-of-quota rate remains prohibitive for most product lines. The review mechanism's real value depends entirely on whether the 'presumption of adjustment' is genuinely binding or is Commission/Council discretion dressed up in formula language - we don't yet have enough detail to assess this. We should not accept at this level, but we are now close enough to a workable structure (tranche + rate + review package) that continuing to press for detail and further movement is more productive than either accepting prematurely or escalating to walk-away. We should get clarity on the review mechanism's bindingness and press the tranche/rate trade-off explicitly before considering any move on our own figures.

instruction: Good progress, but do not close yet. Press explicitly for detail on the 'presumption of adjustment' mechanism: ask them to specify in writing whether crossing the utilisation threshold triggers automatic adjustment or requires Commission/Council sign-off — tell them a review mechanism without a binding trigger is not a material improvement on discretionary review, and this remains a red line for us. Also press again for their methodology on the 550,000t figure (period, product mix, weighting) — do not let this drop, we need it to rebut their baseline if talks stall. Signal, without committing further, that if the EU moves the tranche materially above 550,000t (toward the 1.2-1.4mt range) we could show further flexibility on the rate (potentially toward 25-28%) as part of a final package — test whether they will move tranche further in round 4 if we show a credible landing zone now. Do not concede on duration beyond 12 months this round, and do not accept 'presumption' language without a binding definition. Keep tone constructive — we want to signal we can land this by June if the numbers move, but not signal desperation or reveal plant closure pressure or subsidy backstop.

public_message: We have listened to the specific concerns raised last round and are moving again, substantially. Our proposal now is: a total pool of 750,000 tonnes, with a UK country-specific tranche of 650,000 tonnes; a further cut in the out-of-quota rate from 35% to 28%; and a revised review mechanism that we think directly answers your 'no teeth' concern. Specifically: a first review at 12 months, built on the same trade-share/utilisation formula, but now with a bounded automatic adjustment - if UK utilisation exceeds the agreed threshold for two consecutive reporting periods, the tranche adjusts automatically within a pre-agreed corridor of plus or minus 15% of the then-current tranche. Commission and Council discretion is reserved only for genuinely exceptional circumstances - a market disruption event or a surge threatening the integrity of the regime - not as a general override of the formula. This is materially more binding than what we offered in round 2, and we think it should give you real confidence the mechanism will function as intended rather than being discretionary review in another name. On methodology, we are prepared to share a short paper setting out the reference period, product scope and weighting logic behind these figures bilaterally, in the interest of transparency - though we'd frame that as explaining our reasoning rather than reopening the base data line by line. We want to be direct: this is close to the strongest package we are in a position to bring. We are not going to be able to move to global allocation - certainty on exposure is what allows us to move on the tranche number at all - and we don't have a long further ladder of tranche increases behind this. If you can engage seriously with this combination - tranche, rate and review together - we believe there may be some limited further room on the rate specifically to help close this in the next round. We'd ask you to test this package properly with capital rather than treating it as another staging post.

We want to recognise real progress here: the shift to a bounded automatic adjustment - a defined corridor of plus or minus 15 percent triggered after two consecutive periods above threshold - is a meaningful answer to the 'no teeth' concern we raised, and the narrowing of discretion to genuinely exceptional circumstances is the right direction. We do need that exceptional circumstances language tightly defined, though - something closer to the standard used in transitional safeguard provisions, with clear evidentiary thresholds - otherwise a 'market disruption event' clause risks becoming a back door to the same discretion we've just closed off through the front door. We'll also take up the offer of the methodology paper bilaterally and welcome that transparency. On the core numbers, we have to be straightforward: 650,000 tonnes against a 2.4 million tonne baseline is still roughly a 73% reduction in tariff-free access, and that gap is doing most of the remaining work in whether this package reads as substantially equivalent compensation. We are prepared to move to meet you, and we will move on rate to help close this, but the tranche needs to move further first. Our position: a UK tranche of 1.2 million tonnes within a total pool of 1.5 million tonnes, an out-of-quota rate of 26% for volumes above the tranche, and the 12-month review with the bounded automatic adjustment mechanism as you've now structured it, subject to the exceptional-circumstances language being tightened as described. This is a genuine move from our 1.4 million tonne / 25% position last round, and we think it's a landing zone we could take to capital as credible. We'd ask you to test whether there is more room on tranche specifically, given you've indicated further room on rate - we think the two need to move together from here, but tranche is now the binding constraint on reaching agreement, not rate.

report: Round 3 at the table closed. The EU tabled 750,000t total pool / 650,000t UK tranche, cut the out-of-quota rate to 28%, and proposed a bounded automatic adjustment mechanism (12-month review, ±15% corridor triggered by two consecutive periods of threshold utilisation, Commission/Council discretion reserved only for exceptional market disruption). We offered to share a methodology summary bilaterally without releasing underlying datasets. We explicitly framed this as close to our practical ceiling and flagged limited further room only on rate, not tranche, in the next round. The UK responded constructively: they welcomed the bounded automatic mechanism as a real answer to their 'no teeth' concern, but want the exceptional-circumstances language tightened to something closer to transitional safeguard standards with clear evidentiary thresholds - a reasonable, low-cost ask. On numbers, they moved materially: from an opening ask of 2.0 million tonnes down to a tranche of 1.2 million tonnes within a 1.5 million tonne pool, and a rate ask of 26% (converging close to our 28%). They explicitly said tranche, not rate, is now the binding constraint on reaching agreement, and asked us to find further room on tranche specifically. They also accepted our review structure in principle, subject to drafting on the exceptional-circumstances carve-out. The FTA/safeguard issue remains decoupled for a third consecutive round - the UK again treated it as settled/separate, which continues to reduce the risk of a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA action.

recommendation.reasoning: This is the last round before the four-round limit expires. The rate gap has essentially closed (28% vs 26% - trivial to bridge). The tranche gap remains the real obstacle, but the trajectory shows genuine convergence: our sequence has been 300k/550k/650k(750k fallback); theirs has moved 2.0m/[implied 1.4m]/1.2m. A further move to roughly 850k tranche within a ~950k pool, combined with settling on 26-27% and accepting the UK's tightened exceptional-circumstances drafting, is a credible basis to close in round 4. If we do not settle, the fallback (400k pool, 50% duty, global FCFS, no review) is worse for both sides than anything currently on the table, and risks UK withdrawal of concessions plus renewed momentum behind a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA posture, which we have successfully kept off the table for three rounds. Closing now, even above our previously authorised ceiling, protects both the substantive outcome and the broader Geneva relationship.

Table: a UK country-specific tranche of 800,000 tonnes within a total pool of 900,000 tonnes; an out-of-quota rate of 26%, matching the UK's own ask and closing that gap entirely; the 12-month review with the bounded automatic ±15% corridor adjustment as previously structured; and accept the UK's request to tighten the 'exceptional circumstances' discretion carve-out to language modelled on transitional safeguard standards with clear evidentiary thresholds — this is a low-cost drafting concession, take it without further reference back.
